title: Good decisions begin with trustworthy data: Data sources, capture, integrity, and quality
overview: This week examines how trustworthy data is defined, captured, validated, and monitored. You will distinguish data quality from data integrity and primary from secondary sources, then connect these ideas to the controls and responsibilities of HIM professionals.
objectives: Explain data quality as a continuous concern across collection, entry, storage, and sharing, and describe its characteristics.
Distinguish primary from secondary data sources and data quality from data integrity.
Explain how data dictionaries, metadata, structured fields, edit checks, and required fields support understandable, reusable, and reliable data.
Apply the Define → Capture → Validate → Monitor framework to explain data-quality controls and responsibilities.
Describe HIM responsibilities for protecting data meaning, quality, trust, and workflow.

concepts.name: Data quality
concepts.definition: Fitness of data for use, characterized by accuracy, timeliness, completeness, consistency, accessibility, and validity. Quality control begins at collection and continues through entry, storage, and sharing.

concepts.name: Data integrity
concepts.definition: The trustworthiness of data and preservation of its meaning; supporting controls include identity controls, audit trails, mapping, and validation.

concepts.name: Primary source
concepts.definition: Information recorded directly during patient care or a service.

concepts.name: Secondary source
concepts.definition: Information originally collected for care but later reused for another purpose.

concepts.name: Data dictionary
concepts.definition: A reference defining each data element, including its name, meaning, format, and permitted values.

concepts.name: Metadata
concepts.definition: Information describing data, including when it was created, where it came from, who entered it, and how it should be interpreted.

concepts.name: Structured fields
concepts.definition: Predefined data fields, such as date of birth, diagnosis code, blood pressure, or medication name, that make data easier to validate, compare, search, and analyze.

concepts.name: Edit checks and required fields
concepts.definition: Built-in controls that prevent incomplete or invalid entries, such as requiring a patient ID, rejecting an impossible temperature, or enforcing a date format.

concepts.name: Define → Capture → Validate → Monitor framework
concepts.definition: A sequence for defining the data element and its meaning, capturing it in a usable field or workflow, checking completeness, format, range, and identity, then measuring quality and correcting root causes.

concepts.name: HIM responsibilities for trustworthy data
concepts.definition: HIM professionals explain system purpose; support definitions, standards, terminology, mapping, and consistent interpretation; check data quality; support privacy, security, appropriate access, auditability, and responsible disclosure; and improve workflow through feedback, testing, training, monitoring, and root-cause correction.

sections.body: Data quality is not a final inspection. It begins when information is collected, continues during entry and storage, and remains important when data are shared. Good data should be accurate (correct and free from errors), timely (available when needed and recorded promptly), complete (without important omissions), consistent (used with the same meaning and format across systems), accessible (obtainable by authorized users when needed), and valid (consistent with required rules, formats, and allowed values). These characteristics describe whether data are fit for their intended use. They are related, but not interchangeable: for example, a record may be complete yet not timely, or consistently formatted yet inaccurate.
sections.title: Quality is built throughout the data journey

sections.body: A primary source is information recorded directly during patient care or a service; a nurse entering a patient’s temperature into the EHR during a visit is an example. A secondary source reuses information originally collected for care for another purpose, such as preparing a hospital report, conducting research, or planning staffing. Reuse makes clear definitions and context important. A data dictionary defines a data element through details such as its name, meaning, format, and permitted values. Metadata describes data—for example, when it was created, where it came from, who entered it, and how it should be interpreted. Structured fields provide predefined places for data such as date of birth or blood pressure, helping make data easier to validate, compare, search, and analyze. Edit checks and required fields are built-in controls against incomplete or invalid entries; examples include requiring a patient ID, rejecting an impossible temperature, or checking that a date follows the correct format.
sections.title: Sources, meaning, and controls at capture

sections.body: Data quality asks whether data are fit for use; completeness, timeliness, accuracy, and consistency are examples of quality characteristics. Data integrity asks whether data have remained trustworthy and unchanged in meaning. Identity controls, audit trails, mapping, and validation are examples of controls associated with integrity. The concepts are distinct but related: a system may capture many quality characteristics while still needing controls to preserve correct identity and meaning as information is handled. In the duplicate-record example, a patient is entered twice because the name is spelled differently in two systems. The duplicate records create an integrity problem. Identity matching, verification, duplicate review, data definitions, and exception handling can reduce the risk of unsafe or incomplete information.
sections.title: Quality and integrity answer different questions

sections.body: Use the framework to locate controls and responsibilities across the work: (1) Define the data element and its meaning. (2) Capture it in a usable field or workflow. (3) Validate completeness, format, range, and identity. (4) Monitor quality, measure what is happening, and correct root causes. The sequence helps explain what happens, who is responsible, and where control is needed. It also reinforces that quality work continues after entry rather than ending when a record is first captured.
sections.title: Apply the Define → Capture → Validate → Monitor framework

sections.body: Reliable information depends on purpose and fit, data and meaning, access and trust, and workflow and adoption. Purpose and fit concern whether a system supports intended users, work, outputs, and decisions; scope, workflow fit, and measurable objectives are relevant controls. Data and meaning require information to be complete, valid, consistent, timely, and understood; definitions, metadata, validation, and mapping support that aim. Access and trust involve protecting privacy, security, integrity, and auditability through policy, role-based access, authentication, and logs. Workflow and adoption concern whether people can use information safely and effectively, supported by user testing, training, monitoring, and improvement. HIM professionals connect system purpose to trustworthy information work by explaining purpose; protecting meaning through definitions, standards, terminology, mapping, and consistent interpretation; checking quality; supporting trust and responsible disclosure; and improving workflows through feedback, testing, training, monitoring, and root-cause correction.

activities.title: Respond to duplicate patient records
activities.prompt: Hypothetical application of the duplicate-record example: A patient appears twice in two systems because the name is spelled differently. Which response best addresses the stated data-integrity concern?
activities.debrief: Different name spellings can produce duplicate records and an integrity problem. Identity matching, verification, duplicate review, data definitions, and exception handling are identified controls for reducing the risk of unsafe or incomplete information.
options: Treat the duplicate as a display issue and leave identity review for a final inspection.
Use identity matching and verification, review the duplicate, and apply data definitions and exception handling.
Combine the records immediately without checking identity or meaning.
Focus only on whether the records are complete; do not review how they were matched.

activities.title: Separate quality from integrity
activities.answer: Quality focuses on fitness for use; integrity focuses on trustworthiness and preservation of meaning. The concepts are distinct and may require different, related controls.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes when data-quality control should occur?
quiz.rationale: Quality control begins during collection, continues during entry and storage, and remains important when data are shared.

quiz.question: Which characteristic means authorized users can obtain data when needed?
quiz.rationale: Accessibility means authorized users can obtain data when needed.

quiz.question: A nurse enters a patient’s temperature into the EHR during a visit. How is this information classified?
quiz.rationale: The information is recorded directly during patient care, which defines a primary source.

quiz.question: Patient records originally collected for care are later analyzed to plan staffing. This is an example of:
quiz.rationale: The records were originally collected for care and are now reused for another purpose, which defines a secondary source.

quiz.question: Which resource defines a data element’s name, meaning, format, and permitted values?
quiz.rationale: A data dictionary is a reference that defines each data element, including those details.

quiz.question: Which question is central to data integrity?

quiz.question: What is the correct order in the Define → Capture → Validate → Monitor framework?

quiz.question: At which framework step are completeness, format, range, and identity checked?
